value.overview: The Lesser Ground-Cuckoo (Morococcyx erythropygus) is a secretive, mostly terrestrial cuckoo of dry Central American habitats. It spends much of its time walking or hopping through dense low vegetation, where its brown upperparts and warm rufous underparts provide camouflage. Bright yellow and blue skin around the eye creates a striking facial pattern. Unlike many cuckoos, it builds its own nest rather than regularly laying eggs in the nests of other bird species.
value.classification: The Lesser Ground-Cuckoo belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the order Cuculiformes. It is the only species in the genus Morococcyx.
value.identification: This slender, long-tailed cuckoo is about 25 cm long. Adults have brown upperparts with subtle bronze or greenish reflections, warm cinnamon-rufous underparts, and a dark tail with pale tips on the outer feathers. The bill is yellow with a dark upper ridge, and the legs are yellowish or orange-brown. The eye is surrounded by a yellow orbital ring, with bright blue bare skin behind it bordered by black markings. It is usually detected by its loud, rolling or trilling calls.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from western and southern Mexico through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident, especially on the Pacific slope, where it is associated with the dry lowlands of Guanacaste, the Gulf of Nicoya, and areas around the Tárcoles River. It also occurs locally in the western Central Valley. Typical habitat includes thorn scrub, tropical deciduous woodland, savanna, forest edges, abandoned fields, dense secondary growth, and semi-open woodland, generally from sea level to about 1,200 m.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, not a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals are present throughout the year in suitable Pacific-slope and western Central Valley habitats, although local detectability may vary with season and rainfall.
value.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica generally occurs from February through May. The Lesser Ground-Cuckoo builds a shallow, loosely formed bowl from small sticks, leaf stems, and dry leaves. The nest is placed on the ground, usually behind concealing vegetation in dense scrub or low woodland. A typical clutch contains two chalk-white eggs, and both adults are believed to participate in incubation. Details of incubation length, chick development, and parental care remain incompletely documented.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates. It searches on the ground beneath scrub and woodland, walking, hopping, and making short leaps to seize prey from the leaf litter or low vegetation. Likely prey includes grasshoppers, crickets, caterpillars, beetles, and other arthropods. Because it forages close to cover and is reluctant to fly, it can be difficult to observe even where it is locally common.
value.behavior: The Lesser Ground-Cuckoo is secretive and usually solitary or found in pairs. It moves quietly through dense undergrowth, often pausing before making a short dash or hop to capture prey. When disturbed, it may run or fly only a short distance into cover. Its loud, rolling calls are more conspicuous than the bird itself and may be given from concealed positions. It is primarily active during the day and maintains close contact with dry, brushy ground habitats.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is thought to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
